| [LIT-115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-115.md) v5 | Duality as a category-theoretic concept | Corfield (2015), DOI-10.1016/j.shpsb.2015.07.004. A short programmatic paper. Its thesis is that category theory, not set theory, is the framework in which the scattered instances of mathematical duality can be drawn together. The constructions in §3 (dual adjunctions restricting to dual equivalences on fixed points, truth-value-enriched Galois connections, Isbell conjugation, dualising objects "keeping summer and winter homes") all "revolve around" adjunction, though Corfield expects no "single monolithic account" (p. 59–60). On his usage, 'duality' is reserved for "involution with some form of structural reversal" (p. 57), so several physicists' dualities (homological mirror symmetry as an A∞-equivalence, mirror symmetry's Z2 on the Hodge diamond, S-duality as a vestige of SL(2,Z)) are better called equivalences or symmetries. | [LIT-151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-151.md) v2 | Stating Structural Realism: Mathematics-First Approaches to Physics and Metaphysics | Wallace (2021), DOI-10.1111/phpe.12172. Wallace argues that reading a physical theory "math-first", as mathematical models plus representation rather than as sentences aiming at truth, already makes scientific realism structural. Math-first theoretical equivalence and reduction (as instantiation) are coarse-grained enough to dissolve the standard underdetermination and theory-change objections. On this footing epistemic and ontic structural realism differ only in whether metaphysics itself is language-first or math-first. On math-first OSR, objects are whatever the best "predicate precisification" of a theory quantifies over, real patterns are defined through instantiation plus best precisification, and ontology is scale-relative. At every non-fundamental level the two versions coincide. The paper is explicitly a statement of the position, not a defence of it. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-142.md)); worth reading as the sharpest statement of what structural realism could mean once theories are taken math-first. It gives precise definitions of math-first ESR/OSR and of real patterns, its diagnosis of why priority-thesis OSR drifted is useful, and it is candid about the undeveloped notion of mathematical equivalence it relies on. |
| [LIT-154](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-154.md) v3 | Criteria of Identity and Structuralist Ontology | Leitgeb & Ladyman (2007), DOI-10.1093/philmat/nkm039. Graph theory counts unlabelled graphs whose nodes, or whose isomorphic connected components, cannot be told apart even by an irreflexive relation. Examples are the edgeless two-node graph G′ and any graph with two or more isolated nodes (11 of the 156 unlabelled 6-node graphs). Mathematicians treat these as determinately distinct objects, so the authors conclude that the identity or difference of places in a structure is given by the structure itself, with identity counted among its relations, and not by any criterion of identity. The argument appeals to mathematical practice; it is not a proof. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-133](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-133.md)); worth reading as the short, standard counterexample to weak-discernibility versions of the PII for mathematical structuralism. It is widely cited, and its graph cases are simple enough to check by hand. Its physics coda is explicitly left open. |

| [LIT-222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-222.md) v2 | No categorial support for radical ontic structural realism | Lam & Wüthrich (2015), DOI-10.1093/bjps/axt053. Lam and Wüthrich argue that category theory gives radical OSR no support. Identifying objects with identity arrows is relabelling (§3). Generalized elements X → A exist in every category, so elements are not eliminated (§4). Categories without products also lose set-style relations, "throwing out the relations with the relata" (§4). Morphisms relate C-objects, not the elements that stand for physical relata, and they "only distinguish isomorphism classes of structures" (§5). Bain's GR and TQFT cases eliminate at most spacetime points, not relata tout court (§§6–7). They conclude that category theory "offers little if any comfort to ROSR" (abstract) and favour "balanced" OSR. The Yoneda lemma is not named, although §§4–5 state two of its consequences. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-194.md)); Worth reading as the most careful direct refutation of Bain (yo2). Its main points (generalized elements, morphisms relate C-objects, determination only up to isomorphism, sections are not maximal ideals) are correct and are exactly what the Yoneda reading needs. It has a few category-theoretic slips of its own: Hilb said to lack products, a mis-definition of topos, and the claim that non-commutative algebras have no maximal ideals. |
| [LIT-223](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-223.md) v2 | Category-theoretic structure and radical ontic structural realism | Bain (2013), DOI-10.1007/s11229-011-9896-6. Bain argues that the "relations without relata" objection to radical OSR depends on defining structure set-theoretically, where a relation is a subset of X × X. If a structure is instead "an object in a category", its elements (arrows 1 → A) are "not essential", because category-theoretic objects need not be structured sets. His examples are sheaves of Einstein algebras for GR with asymptotic boundary conditions, which may lack global sections (§3), and nCob and Hilb (§4). He concludes that ROSR "avoids the charge that it rests on an incoherent claim" (p. 1634). The paper never mentions the Yoneda lemma, representable functors or universal properties by name. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-193](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-193.md)); Worth reading as the short, canonical statement of the category-theoretic defence of radical OSR, which the later literature (yo3; Lal & Teh; Eva 2016) responds to.
